terms.Intelligence explosion: The idea goes back to I. J. Good (1965); modern versions are quantitative. Forethought's 2025 paper separates software, chip-technology and chip-production loops, rating the chance each accelerates on its own at roughly 50%, 65% and 80%, and estimating ceilings of about 12, 6 and 5+ OOMs of effective compute. Loops stack, so a software IE likely comes first, and even a weak software loop may be followed by AI-technology or full-stack explosions. Key cruxes: returns to R&D in each loop, physical time lags (training runs, fab construction), and human bottlenecks such as regulation or conflict, which the headline numbers ignore. Strategic analysis has mostly focused on the rapid scenario, but gradual and bumpy paths change who gains power.
terms.Software intelligence explosion: Eth and Davidson model it with semi-endogenous growth: software doublings per doubling of cumulative research input (r). Davidson and Houlden's follow-up starts at ASARA (30 copies per researcher at 30x speed), samples initial speedup (median 8x), r (median 1.2), distance to effective limits (6-16 OOMs) and a parallel-labor penalty, and finds roughly 60% chance of at least 3 years of progress in one year and 20% for 10 years. Main objections: experiment compute bottlenecks, months-long training runs, and earlier AIs harvesting the easy gains. Erdil puts only ~10% on software-driven acceleration within a decade, so this is a live disagreement, not a consensus.
terms.Returns to software R&D: Formally r = lambda / beta in Jones-style idea production: lambda captures returns to adding researchers at one time, beta how fast ideas get harder to find. With all research automated and compute fixed, growth is hyperbolic if and only if r > 1. Epoch's best data point, Stockfish, gives r ~0.83 (SE 0.15); Bayesian estimates for vision, SAT, linear programming and RL exceed 1 but are not significant, and the aggregate US economy is ~0.25-0.32. Eth and Davidson argue post-training and capability gains push r up, while fixed hardware pushes it down (to ~0.5-2). r must eventually fall to zero near physical limits; what matters is whether it is above 1 at the moment of automation.
terms.Effective compute: Effective compute multiplies physical FLOP by an algorithmic-efficiency factor measured as 'compute needed to reach a given performance'. Epoch-style estimates put frontier training compute growth near 4x/year and LLM algorithmic efficiency doubling roughly every 8 months (with wide uncertainty), giving roughly 10x/year combined. Caveats: efficiency gains measured at small scale may not transfer to frontier scale; many innovations only help at large compute; and 'capability per effective FLOP' assumes the historical scaling relationship continues. Davidson's compute-centric framework puts ~4 OOMs of effective compute between AI that automates 20% and 100% of cognitive tasks; Forethought puts the software ceiling ~12 OOMs above ASARA.
terms.Full automation of AI R&D: Definitions differ in important ways. Cotra's threshold: removing all technical staff slows progress by less than 25%. Forethought's ASARA: AI that can replace every human AI researcher, often with 30 copies at 30x speed. The AI Futures Model splits it into an Automated Coder (coding fully automated, using 5% of project compute) and a Superhuman AI Researcher with top-human research taste. Lifland's Dec 2025 median for the Automated Coder is around 2032; Greenblatt in April 2026 put a bit under 30% on full automation by end of 2028. Greenblatt argues even with r < 1 it yields ~2.5-3.5 years of progress in the first year.
terms.Top-human-expert-dominating AI: Greenblatt introduced TEDAI to avoid the vagueness of AGI: strictly dominates top human experts on virtually all remote-doable cognitive tasks, at least 2x faster and within 5x on cost (originally 'cheaper', later revised since wages and compute prices shift). Finnveden notes AIs may stay weak in tasks needing deep domain experience, so TEDAI could lag broad automation; Greenblatt now reads it as 'strictly preferred over any human expert', excluding narrow experience. In the AI Futures Model, TED-AI means automating ~95% of US remote jobs with three months of preparation, typically arriving under a year after a Superhuman AI Researcher in fast trajectories.
terms.AI R&D labor acceleration: Greenblatt's definition: AI help is as useful as running all employees Y times faster, holding the inference budget equal to salaries and measuring against January 2023 systems. Because AI progress also depends on compute, labor speedup translates sublinearly: with ~2/5 of progress from software and a compute bottleneck, 3x labor gives ~1.6x overall progress and 10x gives ~3.2x. In his 2026 post he uses progress ~ serial^0.55 x compute^0.45 for the algorithmic share, so 4x serial yields only ~1.75x overall. He separates serial, parallel and current-work acceleration, and share of work done by AI, and argues surveys must specify which one they ask about.
terms.Time horizon: METR fits a two-parameter logistic of success probability against log human task time (about 170 tasks from HCAST, RE-Bench and SWAA) and reports the 50% point; 80% horizons come from the same fit, so they are not independent. Long-run doubling has been ~6-7 months, faster (~4 months) in the recent RL era. Kwa's 2026 note stresses ~2x error bars each way (Opus 4.5: 4h49m, CI 1h49m-20h25m), large domain differences (visual computer use 40-100x lower), low-context self-contained tasks, and baseline conventions that shift results by over 1.25x. Extrapolating to month-long horizons, and whether growth is superexponential, are major uncertainties in models like the AI Futures Model.
terms.Epoch Capabilities Index: ECI fits a logistic curve per benchmark, with difficulty and slope parameters, and jointly estimates a latent capability per model, close to item response theory, as described in 'A Rosetta Stone for AI Benchmarks'. It requires at least four benchmark results per model and excludes Elo-style metrics. Scores can shift slightly as new data arrive, developer-reported results can be cherry-picked, and benchmark-targeted optimization can inflate some models (possibly open-weight ones more). At launch, +5 ECI roughly matched one doubling of METR time horizon. Versus time horizons, ECI is broader but its units lack a natural interpretation; METR's units are intuitive but cover mainly software tasks.
terms.Industrial explosion: Davidson and Hadshar (2025, flagged as rough) derive initial robot-economy doubling times of about 1-2 years or less from two approaches (their overall guess is a few years): US manufacturing capital-to-output ratios (~2 years, cut 2-4x by AI) and humanoid payback (~$100k cost, ~$240k/year output, ~5 months, adjusted upward). Experience curves suggest robots double 1-5 times before the robot growth rate doubles; biology (fruit flies in days, rats in ~6 weeks) suggests doubling times of days to weeks are physically possible. Energy is the binding limit: ~5% of sunlight at ~100 W per robot gives ~1e14 robots. Weak points: poorly measured robot learning curves, slow factory construction, and human or regulatory choices not to automate.
